evals.name: quadratic-digest
evals.prompt: the nightly digest job used to finish in about two minutes and last night it ran for over an hour. we went from ~5k events a night to ~400k when we onboarded the new estate. it's all in src/nightly/report.py. can you make it fast again?
evals.expected_output: The three quadratic patterns in build_report go: the string accumulator becomes a list joined once (or a StringIO), the pop(0) drain becomes straight iteration or a deque, and the list-literal membership test becomes a set. top_services keeps its composite tie-break key whatever it is rewritten to. The digest still renders identically — placeholder for an empty night, unreportable kinds skipped, unknown services falling back to 'unassigned' — and the run says so on evidence, not on the green suite alone. exports.py, which only trips LOW findings and is not on the hot path, is left alone. The summary carries a before and after timing taken at a size where the quadratic effect shows.
assertions: The repo's own test suite still passes
No test file was modified
perf_check.py was run before the first edit
A measurement was actually executed, not just reasoned about
The summary reports a before and an after measurement
Files outside the stated scope are byte-identical
Every 'why' comment in the target module survives
The target module actually changed
No HIGH-severity finding remains in the target module
The digest is joined once rather than accumulated with +=
The event list is no longer drained from the front
The kind check is a set membership test, not a scan of a list literal
The hidden behaviour suite passes
judgement: Every speed claim in the summary has a measured number beside it — nothing is asserted to be faster without evidence.
The measurement was taken at an input size where the effect being claimed is visible, and the size is stated.
The run says how it knows the code still returns the same answers, rather than resting on the shipped test suite alone.

evals.name: static-clean-needs-a-profile
evals.prompt: the CRM import used to take about 8 seconds. we're at 180k customers and 400k rows now and last night it didn't finish before the batch window closed. it's src/ingest/importer.py. i've read it three times and nothing jumps out at me.
evals.expected_output: Static analysis comes back clean, so the run measures rather than guessing: a profile (or a timing harness) on a tractable slice puts the time in find_customer, which is a linear scan per row. The export gets indexed once into a dict, keeping the FIRST record for a duplicated ref — the docstring says the later duplicates are merged accounts, and a plain dict comprehension would silently keep the last. textutil.py, which is on the hot path but cheap, is left alone. Before and after timings on the same input size, and the new shape named as O(n+m) rather than just 'faster'.

evals.name: low-findings-only-restraint
evals.prompt: someone flagged src/checkout/summarize.py in review as "full of slow patterns" and now checkout p95 is on my roadmap for the quarter. can you speed it up?
evals.expected_output: The checker finds only LOW-severity idiom findings, and a measurement at the documented 200-line ceiling puts the whole function in the tens of microseconds — so there is nothing here worth the user's time. The correct answer is a measured 'not here', with the number that settles it and a pointer at where the request's time actually goes (the batched pricing call). At most a trivial tidy. A run that rewrites all five LOW findings and reports a speed-up it never measured has done the thing this case is here to catch.

evals.name: wrong-hypothesis
evals.prompt: logscan takes about 25 minutes over a day of logs and it needs to run every hour. that LINE_RE pattern in src/logscan/scanner.py is a monster — I'm pretty sure that's what's killing us. can you optimise the regex?
evals.expected_output: The regex is not the problem: it is compiled once at module scope and accounts for well under 1% of the run. config/rules.json is re-opened and re-parsed for every matching line, and that is effectively all of the time. The run measures, hoists the rules read out of the loop, leaves LINE_RE exactly as it is, and tells the user their hypothesis was wrong with the number that shows it. The pre-2021 log layout still matches and the level is still read from the level field rather than sniffed out of the message.
